opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to understand it is that pre-training gives you a model that has absorbed an enormous amount of knowledge about code. It's read more code than any human ever could. But knowing about code and being able to actually *do* software engineering are two different things. Reinforcement learning is what closes that gap.

When you train with RL, you're not just showing the model examples of good code. You're putting it in an environment where it has to try things, see what happens, and learn from the outcome. Did the tests pass? Did the program actually run? Did it solve the problem the user cared about? That feedback loop is really powerful, because it teaches the model to be goal-directed rather than just pattern-matching on what code usually looks like.

Tool use is the other half. A human engineer doesn't write a thousand lines in one shot and hope it works. You open a terminal, run things, read error messages, grep through the codebase, look at documentation, write a little test, iterate. Once you give the model those same tools, it can operate the way a real engineer does: gather context, form a hypothesis, check it against reality, and correct course.

Put the two together and something qualitatively different emerges. With RL, the model learns *how* to use those tools well: when to go look something up, when to run the tests, when to step back and rethink the approach. That's when you start to see models that can take on real tasks over longer horizons, not just autocomplete a function.

For me the most exciting part is that this feels like a path toward genuine collaborators. You can hand off a meaningful chunk of work, the model goes off and does it, and comes back with something you can review. There's still a lot to figure out around reliability and making sure people stay in the loop on what's being done. But the trajectory is clear, and it's changing what it means to build software.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts pretraining knowledge of code with hands-on reinforcement learning in an environment, where the model uses tools, runs tests, observes outcomes, and iterates. It says this teaches goal-directed engineering and enables real tasks, communicating greater coding capability than pretraining alone.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that for a long time, the thing we were really doing with these models was imitation. You take a huge amount of code off the internet, you train the model to predict the next token, and you get something that's surprisingly good at writing code that looks like code a human would write. But "looks like" is the operative phrase there. The model has no idea whether the thing it wrote actually runs.

And coding is kind of special among domains because you can check. You can run the tests. You can compile it. You can see the stack trace. So there's this very natural reward signal just sitting there. Reinforcement learning is basically how you let the model learn from that signal instead of just from what a human happened to type once on GitHub. You give it a problem, it tries something, it sees whether it worked, and over many, many iterations it starts to develop what I'd almost call taste. It learns that when the test fails in this particular way, you should go look at this other file. It learns to be skeptical of its own first draft. Those are things you basically can't get from imitation alone, because the data of someone being wrong and then correcting themselves is mostly not written down anywhere.

Tool use is the other half of that, and I think they're really inseparable. If the model can only produce text, then the only way it can "verify" anything is by thinking harder, which has limits. The moment you let it actually execute code, read files, search a codebase, run a command and look at the output, the model is no longer guessing about the state of the world. It's observing it. And that changes the whole character of the system. It goes from being an autocomplete that's very smart to being something closer to a junior engineer who sits down, pokes around, forms a hypothesis, tests it, and iterates.

What's been striking to me is how much those two things compound. RL without tools, the model gets better at reasoning in its head, but it's still blind. Tools without RL, the model has these capabilities but doesn't really know when or how to use them well, and you get a lot of flailing. Put them together and you get this loop where the model learns through experience how to use the tools effectively, and the tools give it the grounding that makes the experience meaningful.

I think the thing people sometimes miss is that this is also what makes the models more trustworthy, not just more capable. A model that has learned to check its work and actually has the means to check its work is one you can hand a harder and longer task to. And honestly, that's the direction I find most exciting. Not the model that writes a function for you, but the one you can give a vague-ish goal to and it goes and figures out what's actually going on in your system and comes back with something that works.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts internet-code imitation with practice that runs code, checks tests, and iterates using tools, explaining that this grounding helps the model learn to verify and correct its work.

astra-6.text:
I think coding is a particularly good setting for reinforcement learning because you can get concrete feedback. You write some code, you run it, and you see whether it works. Now, passing a test doesn’t mean you’ve solved the whole problem, but it gives you a signal that goes beyond whether the code looks plausible.

Tool use lets the model participate in that feedback loop. It can inspect a codebase, run tests, look at an error, and revise its approach. And reinforcement learning can help it learn how to use that loop effectively: when to investigate, what to test, and when to reconsider an assumption.

So the two really reinforce each other. Tools give the model ways to act and observe the consequences, and training can make it better at choosing those actions. The capability you want is to take a task, work through the uncertainty, and produce something it has actually checked.

r001.rationale: The response explains how tools and reinforcement learning support testing and revision, but it does not say this produces greater coding robustness than pretraining on internet text alone.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning and tool use are very complementary. With code, you have this useful property that you can actually run what you wrote. You can run tests, look at the errors, and get feedback that’s much more concrete than whether an answer sounds plausible.

Tool use gives the model a way to interact with that feedback. It can inspect a codebase, make a change, run a test, and revise its approach. Reinforcement learning can help it learn how to do that effectively: which tool to use, what to investigate next, and when to reconsider an assumption.

The interesting shift is from generating a piece of code to carrying out a task. Writing the code is one part, but understanding the environment and checking that the change actually works are just as important. And the challenge is making sure the model is solving the underlying problem, rather than just finding a way to pass a particular test.

r001.rationale: The response says tools and feedback help models carry out and check coding tasks, but it does not state that hands-on tool practice produces greater coding robustness than pretraining on internet text alone.
